newsitem.title: UK: Gilts prepare for only one poll result--Labour win.
newsitem.headline: Gilts prepare for only one poll result--Labour win.

text.p: A comfortable win for the Labour Party in the British election on May 1 has been priced into gilts for so long that it would take a dramatic upset to cause much of a stir in the market, analysts said on Tuesday.

Analysts said gilts would greet a Labour majority of 70 to 80 seats with a small rally, but were unprepared for three other possible outcomes -- a win by the Conservatives, a small majority for Labour or a hung parliament.

"A hung parliament is the nightmare senario," said Tom Rayner, economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull in London. "The uncertainty raised by such an outcome is phenomenal, so that has to be the most bearish outlook across the board."
Brian Venables, bond strategist at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam, also saw dangers for gilts if there was a hung parliament but dismissed this as unlikely.
A Conservative win was also seen as a long shot, while a small majority for Labour would lead to some weakness for gilts. Instead, many analysts expected gilts to rally on a Labour victory.

"In the short term, I would expect gilts to perform very strongly, but gains to be focused at the long end of the curve because we would expect the new Chancellor to raise rates on May 7 and that clearly will have some short-term impact," he said.
The next monetary policy meeting between the new Chancellor and Bank of England Governor Eddie George is scheduled for May 7.

Interest rate concerns and political worries elsewhere in Europe are expected to overshadow British election results. Gilts are expected to adopt a cautious tone over the next few weeks and are unlikely to move much from current levels.

"There is nothing for the market to get excited about under a change of government but there might be a slight downward bias and then perhaps a recovery from there," said a senior gilts salesman at a major British brokerage.
He forecast gilt futures to be at 108-24 in four weeks' time, little changed from the current level of 109-22.

"Within the first week or so of a new parliament, the market might remain little jittery, with a slight bias to the downside as much as anything else because of international factors," the salesman said.
Some analysts saw the gilt/Bund yield spread widening slightly in the near term, not so much over the election as over possible rate increases.
The gap is currently at 184 basis points, having held within a range of 170 to 192 since January.
The gilts salesman forecast the spread to push out to 195 over the next month.
"With concern about interest rate rises in the UK and the U.S and less of a concern about rate rises in Germany, the spread might just widen a little but not dramatically," he said.
Further out, Rayner saw the spread gap narrowing to 160 basis points, then widening slightly towards the end of the year, if inflationary pressures began to flare up.
But Venables saw the spread narrowing by 20 to 30 basis points post-election.
"Gilts are basically pricing in a Labour victory but they are also pricing in the sheer fact that the economy is very strong and that is going to limit potential short term convergence," he said.
Longer term, he expected gilts to perform best out of the European markets.

"Fundamentals support gilts, as the UK will probably hit the Maastricht criteria more easily than any of the other big European countries," said Venables. "The level of sterling has changed the inflation outlook and I don't think it is as detrimental as it was six months ago. With public finances coming back into more conservative areas, Gilts are set to perform very strongly over the long term."
He said much longer term the spread could slip under 100.
"Fundamentally I don't see why you can't get a spread similar to Denmark," said Venables. The Danish bond/Bund gap is currently at 70 basis points.
